source_text: Περὶ τῆς παραβολῆς τῶν γεωργῶν. Ἰδόντες οἱ σοφοὶ τοῦ λαοῦ τὸν Υἱὸν οὐ πάντη ἀναίσθητοι τῆς ἑαυτῶν ὑπεροχῆς κληρονόμον εἶναι αὐτὸν ὑπειλήφασι· τολμῶσι δὲ καὶ ἀποκτεῖναι ἵνα αὐτοὶ κύριοι τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος γένωνται. Ἐκβαλόντες αὐτὸν ἀπέκτειναν· καὶ εὐθέως ὁ τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος Κύριος ἐπιδημεῖ ἀναστὰς ἐκ νεκρῶν, καὶ κακοὺς κακῶς τοὺς γεωργοὺς ἀπόλλυσιν, ἄλλοις δὲ γεωργοῖς τοῖς ἀποστόλοις παραδίδωσι τὸν ἀμπελῶνα. Εἶτα ἀποκρίνεται ἐκ τῆς προφητείας ὅτι ὑπ’ ἐκείνων μὲν ἀπεδοκιμάσθη, παρὰ δὲ Θεῷ ἐστιν ἔντιμος καὶ κεφαλὴ γωνίας· «Ἀρθήσεται ἀφ’ ὑμῶν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ δοθήσεται ἔθνει ποιοῦντι τοὺς καρποὺς αὐτῆς.»
orientation: Origen is commenting on the parable of the vineyard in Matthew 21, where the wise men of the people see the Son and plot to kill him so they can keep the vineyard.

choices.english: the wise men of the people
choices.why: Literal rendering of the Greek, preserving the ironic designation of the leaders as 'wise'

choices.english: not entirely without perception of their own superiority
choices.why: ἑαυτῶν is reflexive, referring to the wise men's own superiority, not the Son's; they perceived their own eminence was threatened

not wholly unaware of their own preeminence

The verb means 'to be present' or 'to come to a place'; 'arrives' captures the Lord's coming in judgment after the resurrection
Literal rendering of the aorist participle, emphasizing the resurrection as the basis for the Lord's arrival in judgment

pass_b_english: On the parable of the vine-growers. When the wise men of the people saw the Son, they were not entirely without perception of their own superiority, and they supposed him to be the heir. They even dare to kill him, so that they themselves might become masters of the vineyard. They cast him out and killed him; and immediately the Lord of the vineyard arrives, having risen from the dead, and destroys the evil vine-growers utterly, and hands the vineyard over to other vine-growers, the apostles. Then he answers from the prophecy that he was rejected by those men, but with God he is honored and the head of the corner: "The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits" (Matthew 21:43).

problems.why: Greek κακοὺς κακῶς = 'the evil ones badly/evilly.' English 'destroys...evilly' suggests God acts evilly, but κακῶς here means 'severely' or 'in a bad way for them'—the evil ones get bad treatment. The adverb modifies their destruction, not God's manner.
problems.ruling: κακοὺς κακῶς ἀπόλλυσιν means 'destroys the wicked wickedly/severely'; 'evilly' risks implying God acts evilly, misleading readers.

fixed: Changed 'destroys the evil vine-growers evilly' to 'destroys the evil vine-growers utterly': Greek κακοὺς κακῶς means the evil ones are destroyed badly/severely, not that God acts evilly.
